text: Your Honor, this is defendant's motion for summary judgment. This is a pretty straightforward employment discrimination case. Plaintiff is claiming that she was terminated based on national origin and age. She's a Mexican-American female over the age of 40. Your Honor, defendants contend that plaintiff is not able to establish her prima facie case under the McDonnell-Douglas burden shifting analysis. And the fourth element of that prima facie case is that the plaintiff must establish that she was either replaced by someone outside of her protected class or that a similarly situated employee was treated more favorably than her, Your Honor. We believe the evidence shows that the similarly situated employee that Ms. Guerra is trying to utilize is not a similarly situated employee. The Texas Supreme Court is pretty clear on this that for a similarly situated employee, it must be similar circumstances under basically all comparable material respects, including similar standards and conduct and supervisor. And in this case, Your Honor, the evidence and plaintiff does not dispute this evidence that the similarly situated employee that plaintiff is trying to rely on was supervised by a different employee up in Dallas. Ms. Guerra was employed down in Hidalgo County. And so for that reason, it's not a similarly situated employee. And then taking that a step further, the conduct is completely different. Ms. Guerra was terminated based on being unprofessional to her supervisor and she had a prior discipline on her record. The person that plaintiff is relying on is similarly situated. Basically what plaintiff's contending is that this employee was at a company dinner function and in plaintiff's opinion, got drunk and was dancing and she didn't think was being appropriate. Defendant has testified that they did not view what that employee was doing as anything that violated any sort of company policy. And so again, completely different conduct. And for that reason, Your Honor, we would ask her summary judgment be granted because she's not able to establish her prima facie case. If this court believes that she is able to establish her prima facie case, then the burden would shift to defendant to offer a legitimate non-discriminatory reason, Your Honor, and we have done that with the evidence that she was terminated based on a letter from her supervisor that plaintiff was disrespectful and basically not following directives. And for that reason, defendants terminated the employee, which then would shift the burden back to the plaintiff to establish pretext. Or plaintiff has not provided any evidence of pretext. Instead, basically what plaintiff has done is object to defendant's evidence as to their legitimate non-discriminatory reason, Your Honor.
